title: Gyro instruments
object: Gyroscopic flight instruments of a four-seat high-wing light aircraft and their vacuum system: the engine-driven dry pump with carbon vanes, the regulator, the central air filter and the suction gauge; the air-driven attitude indicator cut across its gyro with its pendulous erection vanes, the air-driven heading indicator in plan on its spin axis with its card and setting knob, and the electric turn coordinator cut square to its canted gimbal, with its ball
idea: A fast rotor holds its direction in space, H = Iω: a torque only turns it slowly, at τ/H, so it can carry a horizon and a heading; take away its air and it drifts and topples
summary: A 52 cm³ carbon-vane pump on the engine's accessory pad draws about 53 L/min of cabin air through the central filter and the jets of the two vacuum gyros, and a spring-loaded regulator lets outside air in to hold the suction near 5 inHg (4.1 at idle). The jets spin the attitude gyro's 0.17 kg brass rotor to 21 000 rpm, H = 0.11 N·m·s, so its residual torque wanders it only 0.5°/min while its pendulous vanes unbalance the exhaust jets and erect it at 5.9°/min toward the apparent vertical, which in a turn is tilted (the turn error). The heading gyro, H = 0.065, drifts 2.5° in 15 minutes from its pivots and 11.5°/h more from the Earth's rotation at 50° N, so the pilot resets it against the magnetic compass with the knob. The electric turn coordinator's gimbal is canted 30°, so it feels roll as well as yaw; its rotor's H against a spring gives a deflection proportional to rate of turn, 20° at the standard 3°/s, which at the parent sheet's 110 kt cruise is a 16.8° bank. Its ball lies where gravity and the turn's centripetal pull balance: centred when coordinated, outside in a skid, inside in a slip. When the pump fails the vacuum rotors run down over minutes: as H falls the same small torques turn them faster, the horizon wanders and lies on its stops and the heading creeps, while the electric turn coordinator keeps showing the turn.
usedFor: Pilot training: what each gyro instrument senses, why the heading indicator must be reset, the attitude indicator's turn error, partial-panel flying on the turn coordinator after a vacuum failure, and the ball in a skid and a slip

Physics and engineering courses: angular momentum and rigidity, precession Ω = τ/H, the apparent drift from the Earth's rotation, spring-restrained rate gyros, jet turbines, rotary-vane pumps and pressure regulation

A software-concept explainer: a reference that holds its state only while it is powered, slowly corrected toward a noisy measurement (erection toward the apparent vertical is a complementary filter), and a backup sensor on an independent supply
